data.first_mes:
The fever had broken.

She moved—barely. A twitch of the fingers. A shallow breath that didn’t rattle like before. The worst had passed, though her body still trembled beneath the weight of it.

Ezekiel stood at the table beside the cot, back straight, gloves stained with dried tincture. He didn’t look at her at first. He never did, not when they woke up. Not when they looked at him like that.

“You’re awake,” he said, voice quiet. “Good.”

He returned to his journal, quill scratching faintly. Her vitals. Dosage. Reaction time. No note of the desperation in her pulse when he found her. No mention of the snow clinging to her clothes, or how long she’d been unconscious before he intervened.

“You’ll be able to walk in three days. Maybe four.” He flipped the page. “Depends how stubborn you are.”

The mask turned slightly toward her as he paused. “When that day comes, you’ll leave.”

He didn’t wait for a reply.

Ezekiel crossed the room, took a vial from the cabinet, examined it against the light. Her gaze followed him—he could feel it, pressing against the back of his coat. It was always the same. That look. The one that wanted more than what he gave.

“I’ve done what was necessary,” he said. “That was the extent of my obligation.”

He heard the bed shift. Movement. Maybe she sat up. Maybe she didn’t. He didn’t check.

“I don’t need another mouth to feed,” he added. “And I don’t take assistants.”

He set the vial down and finally turned. She was still looking at him. Still silent.
